title: Who are you? Pronouns and gender
topic: all the personal pronouns; masculine and feminine nouns
why: First lesson of level A1: you complete the set of pronouns (we, you, they, in the masculine and the feminine) and learn how to form the feminine of nouns for people. With job names, you can already say who you are and ask who someone else is, still without the verb "to be."

{"lessons": ["

All the pronouns

You already know אֲנִי, אַתָּה, אַתְּ, הוּא and הִיא. Here is the plural. Just like in the singular, Hebrew distinguishes masculine and feminine everywhere… except for \"I\" and \"we.\"

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
אֲנִיaniI, me
אַתָּה / אַתְּata / atyou (m.) / you (f.)
הוּא / הִיאhu / hihe / she
אֲנַחְנוּanakhnuwe
אַתֶּם / אַתֶּןatem / atenyou, plural (m.) / you, plural (f.)
הֵם / הֵןhem / henthey (m.) / they (f.)

English uses one \"you\" for everything; Hebrew has four: one man, one woman, several men, several women. The plural forms are only for groups: there is no formal \"you,\" so with one person you simply say אַתָּה or אַתְּ. In Israel everyone talks this way, even to the doctor or at the bank.

A mixed group takes the masculine: Avi and Noa together are הֵם. In everyday speech, many Israelis even say אַתֶּם and הֵם to a group of women.

", "

Masculine and feminine nouns

Nouns for people almost always have two forms (like actor / actress in English, but for nearly every word). You can recognize the feminine by its ending:

MasculineFeminineEnding
מוֹרֶה moreמוֹרָה moraa, written ָה
תַּלְמִיד talmidתַּלְמִידָה talmidaa, written ָה
חָבֵר khaverחֲבֵרָה khaveraa, written ָה
סְטוּדֶנְט studentסְטוּדֶנְטִית studentitit, written ִית
מֶלְצַר meltsarמֶלְצָרִית meltsaritit, written ִית
מְהַנְדֵּס mehandesמְהַנְדֶּסֶת mehandesetet, written ֶת
זַמָּר zamarזַמֶּרֶת zameretet, written ֶת

So remember: the feminine ends in a (ָה) or in t (ִית, ֶת). Sometimes a vowel changes along the way, as in מְהַנְדֵּס → מְהַנְדֶּסֶת: learn both forms together.

In the plural, the masculine ends in ִים (im) and the feminine in וֹת (ot):

חֲבֵרִים / חֲבֵרוֹתfriends (m.) / friends (f.) [khaverim / khaverot]
אֲנַחְנוּ תַּלְמִידִים.We are students. [anakhnu talmidim]
", "

Jobs: מִי אַתָּה?

No verb \"to be\" in the present, and no article before a job. English says \"I am a doctor\"; Hebrew simply says \"I doctor.\"

אֲנִי רוֹפֵא.I'm a doctor. (a man speaking) [ani rofe]
אֲנִי רוֹפְאָה.I'm a doctor. (a woman speaking) [ani rof'a]

Watch out, this is the trap for English speakers: in Hebrew, the word changes according to who is speaking. A woman says אֲנִי מוֹרָה, a man says אֲנִי מוֹרֶה.

To ask: מִי אַתָּה? to a man, מִי אַתְּ? to a woman (who are you?). And to say \"me too\": גַּם אֲנִי. The word גַּם goes before the word it goes with.

גַּם אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְטִית!Me too, I'm a student! (a woman speaking) [gam ani studentit!]

מִי אַתָּה? is direct. Among young people at a party, it's natural; otherwise, the easiest thing is to introduce yourself first: אֲנִי…, וְאַתָּה?
